# An Agile New Research Framework for Hybrid Human-AI Teaming: Trust, Transparency, and Transferability

SABRINA CALDWELL and [PENNY SWEETSER](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6543-557X), Australian National University, Australia NICHOLAS O’DONNELL, Queensland University of Technology, Australia MATTHEW J. KNIGHT, Defence Science and Technology, Australia MATTHEW AITCHISON and TOM GEDEON, Australian National University, Australia DANIEL JOHNSON and MARGOT BRERETON, Queensland University of Technology, Australia MARCUS GALLAGHER, University of Queensland, Australia DAVID CONROY, Queensland University of Technology, Australia

We propose a new research framework by which the nascent discipline of human-AI teaming can be explored within experimental environments in preparation for transferal to real-world contexts. We examine the existing literature and unanswered research questions through the lens of an Agile approach to construct our proposed framework. Our framework aims to provide a structure for understanding the macro features of this research landscape, supporting holistic research into the acceptability of human-AI teaming to human team members and the affordances of AI team members. The framework has the potential to enhance decisionmaking and performance of hybrid human-AI teams. Further, our framework proposes the application of Agile methodology for research management and knowledge discovery. We propose a transferability pathway for hybrid teaming to be initially tested in a safe environment, such as a real-time strategy video game, with elements of lessons learned that can be transferred to real-world situations.

CCS Concepts: • **Human-centered computing** → **Collaborative and social computing theory, concepts and paradigms**; **Collaborative interaction**; • **Computing methodologies** → **Cooperation and coordination**; • **Software and its engineering** → **Virtual worlds training simulations;**

Additional Key Words and Phrases: Hybrid teams, human-machine, human-AI, teaming, collaboration, trust, transparency, video games

## 1 INTRODUCTION

Human-AI (or human-machine) teaming offers the potential for achieving decision superiority in a range of environments, including those of a high-risk, time-critical nature. Humans and AI each have complementary capabilities, and effective collaboration could lead to substantial improvements in overall team performance in complex situations. However, the challenges in achieving effective human-AI teaming are numerous and significant. Dellerman et al. [55] noted that while AI is beginning to demonstrate performance in tasks such as autonomous driving, artificial general intelligence solutions that can adapt to change and self-adjust across a wide range of tasks are not yet possible. Instead, the human in a human-AI team is often left to cope with a partner with super-human skills in some areas and a lack of the most basic skills in others.

Given the plethora of unanswered research questions related to human-AI teaming, and the risks inherent in getting it wrong, researchers are attempting to find ways to grapple with this socio-technological field and safely explore hybrid teaming. As a result, development of holistic frameworks and taxonomies around hybrid human-machine teams are attracting attention. Dellermann’s treatise proposes a taxonomy of hybrid intelligence, categorised as human-AI/AI-human interaction, learning paradigm, and task characteristics [55]. This taxonomy describes a number of features of the relationship between humans and AI, as well as the mechanisms by which they learn and the nomenclature of task elements. Dubey et al. [63] also offer a taxonomy of human-AI teaming, focusing particularly on task characteristics, learning paradigms, and teaming properties, and present a proof-of-concept implementation of their **Human-AI Collaboration (HACO)** solution architecture. Seeber et al. [178] identify 819 research questions across 12 domains comprising ideas characterised as affective, cognitive, communication, economic, ethical, organisational, physical, political, societal, social, technical, and others. An important issue raised in their paper is the duality of some of these ideas. For example, they note the duality of positive/negative affect, being the positive or negative emotions a human might feel when an AI agent joins the team.

While it is indicative of the emerging nature of human-AI teaming that these investigations have a strong focus on describing the discipline and naming its parts, even as we attempt to understand what hybrid teams mean for our world, we are advancing towards making them a reality. As such, models become more sophisticated and impactful upon individuals and society. The many questions posed by Seeber et al. [178] and others must be answered. To engage with this complex problem space, we propose that it is necessary to first develop an understanding of the various interacting fields, problems, questions, and related work, and then to model a practical, structured way forward.

In our article, we undertake our investigations through the lens of an Agile iterative develop ment approach. Our goal is to find a path from theoretical research to applied benefits in real-world contexts. We focus particularly on enhanced decision-making and rapid response in potentially high-risk, time-critical situations where the friction between human and AI approaches is particularly visible, and the resolving of that friction is particularly valuable. In this context, safe development and testing environments are crucial, as is practicable transferability from these safe environments to real-world contexts.

We explore how hybrid teams can be practically developed in a considered yet purposeful way, so their introduction into real-world contexts can be safely and effectively accomplished. We employ an iterative process of identifying and deconstructing human-AI teaming elements and exploring the literature to understand the state of each identified element of this nascent discipline. Through this process, we developed a research framework that covers the broad areas of bidirectional situational awareness, human-AI interaction, intelligent decision-making, human-AI operations, and transferability from safe development environments to real-world contexts. Our framework provides procedural context for extant and future research questions relating to implementing human-AI teams for real-world benefits.

We first define our Agile approach to reviewing the literature and developing our framework. We then present broadly-based discussions of trust, transparency, and transferability. We finally present an extended discussion of the elements of our proposed research framework, including an indicative example of how a research project based on this framework and an Agile approach might be undertaken. This work presents the first holistic framework to understand and investigate the complex and varied research questions related to human-AI teaming. Our research framework also incorporates a novel application of Agile methodology for research management and knowledge discovery. With the addition of an Agile implementation approach, our framework has the potential to support and guide advances in hybrid human-AI teaming via mechanisms and structures for enhancing trust, transparency, and transferability to real-world situations.

## 2 APPROACH

In this article, we seek to develop an understanding of hybrid human-AI teaming models and the role of such models in achieving superior team decision-making and operations. By decision superiority, we mean, in general, that the decisions taken by a human-AI hybrid team result in better outcomes than those of humans or AI systems alone. In determining what better outcomes might mean, we note that these would be defined on a project-by-project basis when considering the context and the appropriate tradeoffs of decision-making in that context, such as speed versus accuracy, confidence versus risk, and so on. We employed an Agile approach to arrive at the main themes described in this article, which directed and informed the lower-level literature surveys we conducted. We began by considering the nature of hybrid teaming and the elements supporting the end state of such a pairing: a high-functioning team comprising a mix of humans and AI capable of reaching and acting upon superior decisions, potentially in time-critical or high-risk situations. We then launched an iterative process of identifying the minimum viable aspects to effect the groundwork for such a team, surveyed the literature for an understanding of the state-of-the art with respect to these areas, and built upon that knowledge in a repeating cycle of proposed aspects and literature consultation until we had identified a complete research framework. An important outcome of this approach was the appreciation of the significant roles played by trust and transparency in human-AI teaming, which we then investigated using more common literature survey approaches of key term searches and winnowing.

We further considered the modalities by which human-AI teaming might be safely developed, and then cautiously transferred, to real-world activities. We noted the utility and safety afforded by video games as an environment for developing human-AI teaming without the risk of incurring significant negative real-world consequences. This then led to the final part of our framework, in which we note that lessons learned from video game and other experimental environments might be transferred for use to real-world contexts, while being mindful of aspects that resist simulation. We believe that the breadth and inclusivity of our resulting research framework would not have been achievable without applying the iterative building process of Agile development methodologies from the earliest stages of this investigation.

## 2.1 Agile Methodology

Agile was originally developed as a methodology for software development that arose in the late 1990s as a response to the limitations of the classic waterfall approach in respect of delivering software development projects on time, to scope, and within budget. Waterfall development is a highly formal process in which everything about the final solution is specified in detail before beginning. Large software projects developed in this way were often not fit for purpose and/or outdated before they were (eventually) delivered [114]. Using an Agile approach, software development projects were able to deliver value earlier and more often. The outputs were normally well-suited to the organisations for which they were developed, largely because the organisations had input at every stage to define the purpose and priority of all the features being developed. Agile is particularly useful when the outcomes of development activities are unknown, due to its ability to build upon initial learning and accommodate direction changes and shifting priorities as a result of new learning.

The benefits of the Agile approach to software development were soon seen to be of utility more widely, with organisations such as the Harvard Business Review, McKinsey & Company, and the 2015 Learning Consortium Project endorsing its use in volatile and change-driven organisational environments [56]. The process of Agile development is visually represented in the form of a User Story Map, containing prioritised User Stories. These User Stories set out the answers to the following: “Who wants this feature?”, “What feature is desired?”, and “What is the benefit?” This is embodied in the Agile user story, in which the standard template is “As a &lt;role&gt;, I want &lt;requirement&gt; so that I can &lt;benefit&gt;.” For example, a user story might be “As the human team member, I want to be able to trust the information presented by the AI team member, so that I don’t waste time verifying the accuracy of agent recommendations at the expense of task performance.” Collecting these stories allows Agile teams to prioritise the activities undertaken in a project to ensure that the research and development focuses on outcomes that are of the highest priority and best benefit to the organisation(s) involved [136].

Agile project management is increasingly being adopted by business and government organisations as a way to be more nimble in responding to change [136]. However, the use of the Agile approach as a research methodology is still uncommon, with relatively few researchers introducing Agile methods into their research [84]. For example, Heyer et al. [84] introduced an Agile “research through design” method. Hidalgo et al. [180] explored the underlying challenges and opportunities in using Agile for research, noting the need to relax some of the formal structures in Agile project management to accommodate the necessary flexibility of distributed research teams. Caldwell and Needham [33] adapted Agile for research in a data-driven Government Department, formalising Agile methods for research and the production of new knowledge. We extend upon previous approaches by introducing Agile early during formulating the field for research and weaving it all the way through the research project.

An important consideration in human-AI teaming is to recognise that such teaming cannot be a “one size fits all” scenario. The domain knowledge and professional skills of a cybersecurity specialist are significantly different to those of a medical practitioner or transportation logistics co-ordinator. The desired outcomes to be achieved in these domains will also vary. As a consequence, the AI agent in these domain-specific human-AI teams will have different forms and purposes. We explore Agile as a solution for undertaking an applied research agenda precisely because it can sup port tailored objectives. Through the user story template that requires an understanding of why a feature should be investigated, the answer to whether it is useful and/or appropriate (including whether and how it is transferable to real-world contexts) can also be found.

The work of developing this framework was informed by a particular domain: adversarial operations. This is because we were interested in how a human-AI team might be employed in high-risk, time-critical situations. This domain then guided our consideration of many factors: useful modalities, team characteristics, the potential for shared decision-making, and elements of interpretability and explainability.

## 2.2 Literature Survey

One of the key elements of Agile development is to start small, creating the **Minimum Viable Product (MVP)**, which contains just enough testable progress to ensure that the outcomes are relevant and beneficial. The MVP is then built upon as the project progresses. When applied in research, this approach creates a cycle of building and releasing successive layers of new knowledge and processes.

We incorporated an Agile approach in our literature search and survey, starting first with a more traditional broad-based search to define the current state-of-the-art for human-AI teaming. This search resulted in 135 items.

We then applied the Agile approach to undertake “just-in-time” literature survey activities in respect of how human-AI teaming could be safely developed, and subsequently implemented, in real-world contexts to manage complex, time-critical and/or high-risk situations. “Just-in-time” is a key theme of Agile, in which effort is constrained to the goal immediately at hand. This allows effort to be focused on meaningful tasks, to maximise the amount of (unnecessary) work not done.

These additional literature reviews informed a third (traditional) stage of the literature review, in which we used key terms relating to the user stories developed in Stage 2 to iterate from the first layer of investigations to the more focused areas identified in our Agile investigation of this research space. Ultimately, the scope of our literature survey across all of the relevant domains encompassed 226 articles. Our Agile approach to our literature survey is described in this section and illustrated in Figure 1.

## 2.2.1 Stage 1. A literature survey was undertaken to investigate the research question:

How can a hybrid human-AI team collaborate in experimental environments to achieve operational efficiency and decision superiority, and how can elements of such collaborations be transferred from experimental environments to real-world contexts?

Our first step was to perform a traditional literature survey. Potential records in the literature related to human-AI teaming were sought, largely through searching key terms in Google Scholar, and potential articles were identified, then further filtered via article titles, abstracts, and year of publication. The number of articles in the resulting Stage 1 literature was 135. The terms and keywords used in Stage 1 of the literature review can be seen in the Appendix.

2.2.2 Stage 2. Closer inspection of the chosen articles from Stage 1 provided more detail of the concepts being discussed in the literature in relation to our research question. These articles were useful in describing the research landscape. However, it quickly became clear that hybrid teaming was in very early stages of development, with a need for a way for all of the various elements to cohere into a blueprint for developing hybrid teaming from embryonic ideas to high-functioning, real-world teams. Recent advances in Agile [33, 84, 84] suggested that a useful approach to identify ing pertinent features of a research-focused activity was through the use of Agile methodologies, specifically identifying “who needs what and why.” These user stories, of which there might be many, can be coalesced into similar requirements, or research areas, and arranged from left to right in terms of the likely chronological order.

In the case of this literature investigation, the goal(s) immediately at hand were identified via epic user story generation based on a combination of questions extant in the literature and considering how the questions impacted upon practical implementation of a hybrid team. Epic user stories are stories that are complex and need to be decomposed into sub-parts small enough to be actionable.

Remembering that a user story takes the form of “As a &lt;role&gt;, I want &lt;requirement&gt; so that I can &lt;benefit&gt;,” we began by considering the roles that might be involved in a hybrid team. Some examples we identified were human team member, command and control member, auditor, and user/beneficiary, Examples of these epic user stories are “As a human team member I want to be alerted to any ambiguities or inconsistencies in bi-directional communication schema of the team so that I can avoid taking a decision based on inappropriate information,” “As a command and control member I want to be advised of task completion so that I can delegate new tasks,” and “As a beneficiary of the human-AI team operations, I want to be provided with explanations for decisions taken by the hybrid team, so that I can understand why decisions affecting me have been taken and raise any issues.”

A particularly interesting role was that of the AI team member. Using language that attributes human-like aspects to the AI member can be a useful device, so long as we are careful to remember it is not actually human, and it was valuable to formally identify this role as a stakeholder, as it raised new and interesting user stories. Examples of these are “As an AI team member, I want to have access to established protocols for decision-making so that I can accurately assess the boundaries of my authority to take and enact decisions” and “As an AI team member, I want a mechanism to accurately identify and assess the state of my human team member, so that I know that the team is not compromised and can validly operate.”

This phase resulted in five general research areas. The first four of these five areas, bi-directional situational awareness, human-AI interaction, distributed decision-making, and human-AI opera tions, related to hybrid team development in an experimental environment. The last area, transferability, was identified as the final stage in hybrid team development: transferring knowledge of hybrid teams to real-world contexts. These five areas comprise the backbone of our research model.

With the research backbone established, the next step was to identify a “walking skeleton,” or the bare minimum research and development needed to create prototypical hybrid teams across the research backbone fields. Arranged in order of priority, it created an end-to-end description of the sub-categories of research and development, forming a path from inception of a hybrid team to transferal of hybrid team knowledge and processes to the real world. Again, user stories were written, in conjunction with knowledge conferred through the traditional literature review of Stage 1 and the initial part of Stage 2. The elements of the walking skeleton were identified (Figure 1) and these new areas of investigation were fed into Stage 3.

2.2.3 Stage 3. In Stage 3, the key terms of the research backbone and walking skeleton were searched in Google Scholar, and additional articles were identified and filtered as with Stage 1. A further 91 records were found of relevance to our now elaborated research question and examined more closely to understand the state of knowledge in respect of the Agile research framework established. This total of 226 items varied slightly in subsequent reviews with five papers being added and 14 being removed, resulting in a total of 217 items. This final body of literature was mapped against the five areas identified as set out in Table 1. The terms and keywords used in Stage 3 of the literature review can be seen in the Appendix.

## 3 TRUST AND TRANSPARENCY IN HUMAN-AI TEAMS

While the literature survey identified five research areas, or epics, that are key to researching and developing a successful human-AI team, it is important to note that all of these areas are impacted either directly or indirectly by the trust humans have in their AI team member, and interestingly, the trust an AI agent can put in its human team member. Trust is a pervasive background context to all elements identified in our research backbone and sub-categories, and therefore, we first consider trust and its foundational partner, transparency, in the context of human-AI teaming.

Trust between humans and autonomous systems is composed of a dynamic “complex of multi ple processes that are parallel and interacting” [86] that can vary over time [125]. That complexity is underlined by the conditional nature of the trust between humans and machines. The “machine is trusted to do certain things, for certain tasks, in certain contexts” [86]. In performing those tasks, that trust can dynamically develop, mature, strengthen, deteriorate, and be repaired [52, 86, 125]. The dynamic nature of trust development and maturation can be observed over three distinct phases. Initially, the trust in the system is based on the predictability of the system’s behaviour. Over time, trust increases when the automation has proven its dependability. Finally, after prolonged interaction with the system, the operator develops faith in its future behaviour [125, 168].

Trust in autonomous systems can have multiple modes, from the default trust most people have in everyday technology through to the deliberate trust placed in other technologies. Trust in tech nologies is nuanced and includes consideration given to what the conditions for trusting that sys tem might be [86]. For expert users of autonomous systems, trust tends to be deliberate. Experts think carefully about whether to trust the system and under what conditions [86]. Those users can then calibrate that trust within the boundaries of whether to trust or mistrust the system and whether that trust or mistrust is justified or unjustified based on their understanding of the system’s competencies, reliability, and integrity [51, 70, 86, 125]. At the same time, they balance their appetite for risk in using the system and the uncertainty of surrendering control [125, 183].

Within Human-AI teams the calibration of trust can be bi-directional, with both the human and the autonomous agent actively exploring trustworthiness by verifying whether to take the other’s declarations as true and verifying the reasons to carry out instructions [51, 86]. Indeed, the ultimate form of trusted autonomous teaming incorporates bi-directional trust [1]. The human trusts the machine (human-machine trust) and, while not in the same way as humans, the machine trusts the human (machine-human trust). This bi-directional trust is essential to ensure that autonomous agents can perform effectively in their intended role and that their performance will not result in “high-regret, unintended consequences” [51]. Similarly, bi-directional trust is essential to ensure that humans perform their role effectively within the team by neither disusing (under-reliance) nor misusing (over-reliance) their autonomous teammates [46, 71, 125, 158].

## 3.1 Factors Affecting Trust in Human-AI Teams

System properties, operator properties, and environmental factors can all impact the trust relationship within human-AI teams [125]. System properties that can affect trust include three of the key components used by humans to calibrate trust: competency, reliability, and integrity [51, 125, 183]. Other properties that affect trust include auditability (the system is able to preserve and communicate its record of reasoning), predictability (avoiding aberrant behaviour; potential system faults are known to the operator), directability (humans can intervene to correct a behaviour), intelligibility (the system is able to explain its reasoning), ineffective interfaces (impacting communication between teammates), and a lack of self-awareness (e.g., system health). The system’s level of automation also affects trust, as systems with greater autonomy tend to be more complex and less transparent [51, 125, 183]. This opacity highlights the importance of causability tracing, in which the system is able to provide an acceptable quality explanation to tie together the cause of the system’s determination and human-intelligible reporting to support human decision accountability [89, 90]. Operator properties that can affect the trust relationship within Human-AI teams include: the operator’s propensity to trust (their attitude towards autonomous systems), individual differences between operators (e.g., motivation and self-esteem), and cultural differences, such as the difference between high-power distance societies (slow to repair trust) and low-power distance societies [125]. Environmental factors that can impact the trust relationship include risk (high risk versus low risk) and uncertainty about the operating environment [125, 183].

## 3.2 Measuring Trust

Measuring trust in autonomous systems is challenging and is made even more difficult in a dy namic, moment-to-moment situation, as operators respond in real-time to changes in the system’s competencies, reliability, and integrity. Lewis et al. [125] identified a number of existing validated measures developed to measure trust in automation. Some measures, such as the **Empirically De rived (ED)** instrument [100], measure the propensity to trust rather than trust within a specific system. Conversely, other measures such as the cross-cultural measure of trust measure both the propensity to trust pre-experiment and take repeated measures of trust in the system to measure the effects of manipulations designed to impact trust [41, 42]. Recently, Holzinger et al. [89] formulated a **System Causability Scale (SCS)** to rapidly assess the link between causes and decisionsupport explanations generated by AI/human-AI systems. This approach is based on the widely used **System Usability Scale (SUS)** designed to rapidly assess the usability of a system. The SCS comprises a list of 10 statements about the quality of the system’s explanation, assessed by a hu man on a five-point Likert scale, thus converting qualitative views of the explanations to a numeric outcome that indicates where on the scale of causability the system under investigation is placed [89].

While psychometric instruments (e.g., trust measures [41, 42]) are valuable, as they can provide the most direct measure of trust in the system, they are also intrusive and not typically suitable for measuring trust mid-task [125]. One method for supplementing these measures to build a more complete picture of the human operator’s trust in the system and the quality and resilience of the trust relationship within a hybrid team is to incorporate a range of physiological measures (e.g., **heart rate (HR), electro-dermal activity (EDA)**, and **brain electrical activity (EEG)**). These measures can be used to assess the emotional, physical, and cognitive impacts of manipulations designed to impact the trust relationship. Physiological measures are indirect indicators of trust, rather than direct measures, and can be effectively used alongside psychometric instruments.

3.2.1 Trust Engineering. Given the dynamic, complex nature of trust, designers of autonomous systems should be wary of aiming for a simple “single stable state” of trust. Rather, designers should be seeking to achieve an “appropriate expectation” of trust within the system [86], calibrated through the process of active trust management [70]. Active trust management entails the continuous assessment of a range of measurable trust elements (e.g., competence, predictability, dependability) to ensure system trustworthiness. Hoffman et al. [86] characterised the methodological challenges facing autonomous system designers seeking to incorporate active trust management into autonomous systems as the “active exploration for trusting.” They identified trusting challenges for system designers, such as how an autonomous system might mitigate unjustified trust and mistrust or support trust calibration in new and/or unusual settings. They also identified the need to both speed up and simplify the trust analysis process for operators, so a system might be able to promote swift and justified trust while simultaneously reducing the cognitive load on operators in high-risk, time-critical environments.

One study posited the development of heuristics to support trust, implementing a set of six cognitive heuristics (reputation, endorsement, consistency, self-confirmation, expectancy violation, and persuasive intent) that were shown to successfully support the evaluation of the credibility of online information [140, 141]. Additional collections of heuristics have also demonstrated their adaptability and fitness in other related contexts, including estimating trust between agents within multi-agent systems [169], judgemental forecasting [6, 167], and HR management [93]. Within hybrid teams, these heuristics might have the potential to facilitate bi-directional trust and transparency and could potentially be integrated within the interface between the human and autonomous agent teammates [22, 51, 52, 128, 129].

3.2.2 Trust Repair. To better understand the complex nature of human-autonomous systems, we might need to reframe our understanding of such systems as being beyond interactions and towards more of a relationship [52]. This is especially true for the dynamic nature of the trust relationship between humans and autonomous systems, which incorporates not just the initial development of that trust relationship, but also potential strategies for repairing the trust relationship after a trust-deteriorating event. Early research has identified that trust repair between humans and autonomous systems mirror those of human-to-human relationships, and mistakes made by autonomous systems are assessed similarly to mistakes made by humans [118]. This research has also demonstrated that human-to-human methods of trust repair such as causal attribution [194], which reveals that well-timed apologies are more effective than explanations, denials, and assurances of control, are equally effective in repairing trust between humans and autonomous systems [110, 118, 171].

3.2.3 Physiological Measures of Trust. Physiological measures such as **heart rate (HR), electrodermal activity (EDA)**, or **electroencephalograms (EEGs)** are indirect indicators rather than direct measures of trust and might be affected by unrelated causes, which means we need large amounts of training data for our AI systems. For any one-time instance, only a probabilistic prediction is possible of the degree of trust. Once sufficient ground truth data is available, either through post-facto application of psychometric instruments or deduced from behavioural clues (such as more or less hesitance or delay in acting in response and so on), AI approaches can pre dict many human internal states to a surprising degree, and it is likely that this could be the same for trust. In a number of cases of predicting internal states, once the mapping from physiological signals to ground truth is learned, the prediction accuracy from physiological signals can be higher than from verbal responses from the same participants. Examples are emotion veracity of smiles [91] and detection of deceit and subjective doubt [217].

## 3.3 Elements of Transparency

Transparency between humans and autonomous systems is intended to ensure that human operators have an understanding of the autonomous systems’ behaviour, reliability, and intent [22, 128]. This transparency plays a vital role in assisting humans to calibrate their trust in autonomous systems [128, 206] for them to work together effectively [39]. Understandably, as autonomous systems become more complex and the system’s behaviour becomes more autonomous, the importance of transparency also increases [111, 128]. However, as AI systems have become more complex, the trend so far has been for transparency in decision-making to decrease, for example in the use of deep neural networks [97].

3.3.1 Models of Transparency. While many of the early conceptualisations of transparency within human-machine teams were focused solely on robot-to-human factors (information the robot needed to share), more recent conceptualisations have also factored in robot-of-human transparency (information the robot has about the human), which is exemplified in the Lyon’s models of transparency [128]. The Lyon’s models suggest that the human should have access to information on the agent’s intentions (purpose), tasks (actions), analytics (decision-making), and environment (operating conditions). In addition, the overall performance of the human-machine team benefits from the machine having awareness and understanding of a range of human factors (e.g., health, cognitive workload, emotional state). Finally, the teammates should also have a shared understanding of each other’s roles and tasks [128].

The **Situation Awareness-based Agent Transparency (SAT)** model is another model of transparency [40]. The SAT was developed to provide a framework for what information should be communicated to operators by the agent (robot-to-human) to promote transparency [40] and facilitate effective shared decision-making [39]. The original SAT model was composed of three levels to aid the human’s perception, comprehension, and projection of the agent’s behaviour:

(1) Goals and actions: the purpose, intent, progress, and performance of the agent;

(2) Reasoning: the agent’s reasoning process when planning its actions; and

(3) Projections: predictions, levels of uncertainty, and likelihood of success/failure around future outcomes.

The original SAT model was subsequently revised and expanded to incorporate aspects of teamwork transparency and bi-directional communication between operators and agents [39]. Similar to the Lyon’s models [128], the incorporation of human-state information and teammate awareness via bi-directional communication and the resulting bi-directional transparency was seen as essential for accommodating the increasingly dynamic nature of human-agent interactions to maintain a team’s effectiveness [39]. By incorporating bi-directional transparency alongside bi-directional trust within a Human-AI team, humans and autonomous agents are able to share each other’s understanding [22]. This shared understanding allows the human and the autonomous agent to draw upon each other’s intent, performance, capability, planning, and reasoning practises [22] to inform their own decision-making processes [39].

## 4 TRANSFERABILITY

Similarly to trust, transferability has a special role in this investigation of human-AI teaming, in this case from the perspective of utility. We consider here how human-AI teaming can be modelled in a safe environment for purposes including high-risk, time-critical scenarios. Therefore, we then necessarily must consider how the learning gleaned from this safe environment can be made use ful in real-world contexts. Some consideration is then required of transferability as an end-goal, a critical process, and an outcome that must be supported by all of the research preceding its implementation. We define transferability as the ability to transfer findings from an experimental environment to a real-world context. Transferability entails considerations of knowledge transfer, the experimental environment, and evaluating which outcomes are transferable. To be effective, it also requires an alertness to the limitations of the experimental environment. In this section, we discuss knowledge transfer and exchange, affordances of experimental environments, with a particular focus on game environments and evaluation via metrics and measures.

## 4.1 Knowledge Transfer and Exchange

**Knowledge transfer and exchange (KTE)** is an interactive process for exchanging meaningful knowledge between research producers and research users [109, 144]. The primary aims of KTE are to ensure that the knowledge produced is used by decision-makers, policymakers, planners, and practitioners to support evidence-based policy and decision-making. It additionally enables researchers to identify relevant fields of enquiry within the problem space [109, 144]. The challenge for research producers and research users partnering to explore a problem space is in being able to identify a suitable strategy for KTE that meets the project and the partners’ needs [109, 122, 144].

Lavis et al. [122] developed an organising framework for a knowledge-transfer strategy between researchers and decision-makers based around five key questions:

(1) What should be transferred (the message)?

(2) To whom should it be transferred (the target audience)?

(3) By whom (the messenger)?

(4) How should it be transferred (processes and supporting communication infrastructure)?

(5) And with what effect (performance measures to evaluate success)?

Lewis’ approach proposes that actionable messages (1) based on ideas that can impact the prob lem space are preferred by decision-makers over simple research reports or the results of individual studies composed of data [122, 208]. The target audience (2) for the message needs to be clearly identified and the knowledge transfer strategy needs to take into account the types of decisions they make and the environment in which those decisions are made. When seeking to identify the target audience, researchers need to consider not just who can act on the transferred research knowledge but also who can influence those that act [122]. The credibility of the individual, group, or organisation (3) delivering the message (i.e., the research knowledge to be transferred) is critical to the success of the knowledge transfer [122, 181].

It can often take considerable time for relationships to develop to the extent that the research team is considered a trusted source, and in some cases there is merit in having the researchers conduct the knowledge transfer through a trusted intermediary [122]. Interactive engagement with the target audience is the most effective method of transferring knowledge (4), which is pre-ferred over passive processes that tend to be less effective. This interaction can happen in multiple stages, and over longer periods the “two-way exchange” can result in bi-directional knowledge transfer that has the potential to produce cultural shifts on both sides of the exchange [94, 122]. Performance measures to evaluate the success of the knowledge transfer (5) are important. Where possible, measuring knowledge transfer outcomes should look to capture how that knowledge has been used and not just whether the knowledge was used [122, 207]. For example, was the research used in an instrumental way (i.e., used to solve a specific problem)? Or was the research used in a conceptual way (i.e., as a more general form of illumination of the problem space)? Or was the research used in a symbolic way (i.e., used to justify a position already held or an action already taken [20, 122])?

Ebener et al. [65] take a similar approach to knowledge transfer as Lavis et al. [122] by organising their framework around a series of questions designed to clarify the knowledge type, the knowledge flow, and the participants in the knowledge transfer. However, the Ebener et al. framework [65] also incorporates a series of knowledge maps—a visual association of items of information [199]—to help identify any potential gaps between the theoretical and the actual knowledge translation processes. This comparison helps to identify any opportunities for improvement to the actual process and is a precursor to understanding the impacts of those differences on the knowledge transfer process itself.

## 4.2 Affordances of the Experimental Environment

Selection of a simulation environment is a crucial decision in any project. The nature, properties, and affordances of the environment can have a strong influence on the types of experiments that can be carried out and the research questions that can be investigated. In AI research, ideal environments for development and testing allow for repeatable experiments and provide extensive control over relevant environmental features and parameters. Video games have proven to be effective and appropriate environments for progressing the development of AI algorithms, with a wealth of previous AI research applied to video games [18, 19, 203]. Complex **real-time strategy (RTS)** games offer considerable benefits as simulation environments and AI test beds [75]. RTS games include many elements related to areas of real-world interest, including resource management, decision-making under uncertainty, and collaboration [30].

Different research questions will require different affordances in video game or other simulation environments used for development and testing. However, there are some common considerations:

• API: Does the environment include an **API (Application Programming Interface)** to al low for AI development and testing?

• Complexity: Is this environment challenging for both humans and AI?

• Tooling: Are there already good tools for working with this environment? Is it likely that this environment will be supported in the future?

• Customisation: Can this environment be modified easily? Is there control over the complexity of the game?

• Suitability: Is this environment inherently suited to the research problem with minimal modification?

• Community: Is there a body of research in this environment in the literature? Is there an active community of players?

4.2.1 Modes of Interaction. We look here at choice of mode of interaction from both the humanto-machine direction and the machine-to-human direction and discuss how these choices might effect transferability to real-world domains.

Human-to-machine. Human interaction with video games has been predominantly via 2D graph ical user interfaces or from 3D first-person perspective. These modalities typically use traditional input devices such as a keyboard and mouse or game controllers. More recently, the methods by which humans interact with games have been expanded to include virtual reality, mixed reality, augmented reality, and voice and gesture. Microsoft Kinect has played an important role in providing accessible gesture recognition [81]. Even brain-computer interfaces have been studied on surprisingly complex games [176]. The plethora of interaction modalities gives research designers an important choice about how human subjects interact with the experimental environment. For RTS games, traditional input methods such as keyboard, mouse, and game-controller are likely es sential for high precision and low latency play. However, supplementing these input devices with gestures, voice, and others could provide interesting multi-modal interactions [198]. For example, a user might play the game with the mouse and keyboard but interact with an AI using voice. Passive interaction is also possible, for example, an AI monitoring and responding to the user’s heart rate.

Machine-to-human. While human interaction with the system is constrained by the environment’s precision and response time requirements, the same is not true for the machine’s interac tion with the human. Communication by text [172], voice [151], and contextual hints [45] have all been explored in the literature with promising results. In addition to these, an RTS environment lends itself to direct interaction with the game elements themselves, such as highlighting units, marking map locations, or even managing low-level control of units. As with human interaction, a design where an AI makes use of multiple modalities to communicate with the user could be possible.

Effect of Modality Choice on the Transferability of Environment. The choice of modality creates some potential challenges relating to transferability into real-world settings. The challenge of using novel means of input might present interesting challenges in a computer game setting [153]. However, the lack of precision, user familiarity, and specialised hardware make novel input devices less suitable for research that is intended to be integrated into real-world applications.

## 4.3 Metrics and Measures

The generation, capture, and analysis of data derived from experimental settings is critical to successfully transfer the knowledge derived to real-world scenarios. Depending on the environment, along with potential metrics and measures identified in the research planning process, the breadth and depth of that data can be substantial. Simulating real-world complex situations amenable to hybrid human-AI teaming within complex, RTS video games in experimental settings has two significant advantages over investigations of human-AI teaming outside the RTS video environment. First, games can capture the same data as their analogue equivalent, in addition to a considerable range of performance measures, such as game play metrics (e.g., actions per minute, decision points, outcomes) across multiple, iterative, scenario sets. The second major advantage is the sheer volume of scenarios that can be run within complex, real-time video game investigations of com plex issues within relatively short time frames.

In addition, experimental settings allow for generation and capture of data that relates specifically to the experience of the participants throughout the simulation. Potential participant data includes quantitative psychometric measures (e.g., trust, stress, coping, teamwork) and biometric measures (e.g., **heart rate (HR), electrodermal activity (EDA), brain electrical activity (EEG)**). This allows us to indirectly assess the emotional, physical, and cognitive impacts of the experimental settings designed to explore aspects of the human-AI teaming experience. Qualita tive data is also helpful to support interpretation of quantitative data and to elicit human reflection upon aspects of their experience.

4.3.1 Verisimilitude of Experimental Settings. The use of a number of scenarios with increasing verisimilitude or similarity to real-world settings and their differential effects of biometric measures can be used to assess the degree of transfer likely to be achieved. That is, if the changes in biometric measures increase with increasing verisimilitude, but then reach a plateau, then we can conclude that further increases (up to actual reality) will not cause different reactions and hence the behaviour in the simulation will transfer to the real setting. This has been observed in relatively low-to-mid fidelity driving simulators, where the biometric measures vary differentially with increasing verisimilitude. For emergency situations, there is a plateau at a surprisingly low level of verisimilitude [95].
