## 5 PROPOSED RESEARCH FRAMEWORK

In this section, we present a proposed framework for conducting research into hybrid human-AI teaming. After our initial literature survey to determine state-of-the-art in human-AI teaming, we applied the Agile approach to develop our research framework, supplemented by additional “just-in-time” literature survey activities with respect to how human-AI teaming could be safely developed and subsequently implemented in real-world contexts to manage complex, time-critical, and/or high-risk situations. This resulted in the research framework illustrated in Figure 2, which we explain in the following sections. This framework provides a structure within which future re search in hybrid teaming can be organised. As each prototypical hybrid teaming element becomes well understood along the path of the walking skeleton, a minimum viable hybrid team can ultimately be produced and incrementally built upon. For each element in our framework, we consider current thinking and propose some initial research questions arising from our investigations.

## 5.1 Bi-directional Situational Awareness

To successfully complete any goal, a team requires an understanding of the situation in which they find themselves, or “what’s going on around them.” Managing situational awareness in hybrid teams offers opportunities to leverage the resources and affordances of significantly different team members. However, some of the same challenges of human-human teams, such as information overload leading to degradation of situation awareness [135], exist in hybrid teams, though in a different form. In addition, AI is usually not designed for interpretability and transparency, nor does it leak information by its behaviour in the way humans do, so humans cannot be as AI-aware as AI team members can be human-aware [200]. Conversely, retrieving information from humans can be subjective and error-prone, so it is likely that human and AI each only ever has a partial view of the other [187]. Bi-directional situational awareness in our research model comprises sensing, communication, and schema.

5.1.1 Sensing. In a given scenario, both human and AI team members must first collect information about the environment and circumstances of the situation. Humans rely on their vision, hearing, and cognition to understand and respond to events unfolding in a video game. Cognition plays at least two roles. First, cognition, which includes memory, reasoning, and attention, is necessary to learn, remember, and apply instructions. Second, it has been shown that cognition and visual perceptional learning are linked as a form of adult plasticity, in which gameplay experience increases white-matter connectivity within the brain and increases gaming performance [113]. An AI team member senses its environment in a video game through the acquisition and processing of data about the game. Once team members have collected information, they must communicate it to each other to ensure that each member has the fullest, most current and, importantly, most relevant information available to inform their planning and decision-making.

Potential research questions include: How can the differing capabilities of human and AI sensing be used to create the optimal fusion of information? What are the most effective strategies for a hybrid team being able to identify and track threats and opportunities? How can hybrid teams filter data to determine key elements of situational awareness information? What are the most effective strategies for identifying emerging opportunities and threats within the game environment?

5.1.2 Communication. There are many precursors for communication involving AI, such as home assistants Alexa and Siri, and GPS navigation, but communication is yet another area of hy brid teaming that is in a nascent state. We already know that communication relating to systems is fraught with error. For example, the Iran Air Flight 655 disaster, where 290 civilians lost their lives when their Airbus A300 was destroyed by a surface-to-air missile fired from USS Vincennes during an engagement with Iranian F-14s was an example of systems involved communication failure. The disaster could have been averted by either the Vincennes communicating with the the Airbus A300 or the Airbus A300 having transmitted their status as a civilian aircraft, depending on which version of the story is to be believed [1]. Clearly, communication is already noticeably complex, let alone as researchers attempt to transition from well-established models of human-human communication and understand how those models relate to human-machine interaction. What happens when humans stop asking “With whom am I communicating?” and start asking “With what am I communicating” [80]? Recently, a research agenda for this element of hybrid teaming proposed that human-AI communication is characterised by three aspects: functional dimensions such as how humans understand the machine(s) with which we communicate, relational dynamics, or human relationships with these machines, and metaphysical blurring of ontological boundaries [80].

An additional dimension, implicature, has been proposed by Liang et al. [127] to be particularly relevant to AI communication in video games. Implicature is the process by which humans infer more from words that are spoken than the simple meaning of the sentence. We can imply and infer based on what is said, when it is said, and the context in which it is said. AI has yet to attain this social skill, which is further complicated by many aspects of context being dynamic and resistant to modelling. This dictates that, at present, commands given to an AI team member must be clear and given without expectation that underlying meanings will also be communicated.

Potential research questions include: What human information processing characteristics are most easily utilised in hybrid teams to reduce cognitive load on human team members? What robot-of-human information is a human comfortable sharing with the machine teammate within a hybrid team?

5.1.3 Schema. The term schema is used in various ways in different disciplines. Here, we refer to the core ideas of a schema: organised relationships between units. At its most basic level, a schema for hybrid teaming would contain the units such as {human, machine, information}, with the relationships between these units defined. A human-AI schema can be conceptualised as existing at increasing levels of sophistication, from uni-directional information transmission to collaborative teaming [200]. For example, in an RTS game, a player could make the over-arching strategic decisions but leave the fine details to automated control. Or, conversely, an AI could make overaching strategic decisions and let the human implement them. These two schemata have very different implications in terms of the safety and reliability of the teaming system. Within an RTS game, the worst that could happen is the player loses the game, while in a real-world context the outcome might be more dire. Perfecting the schema within the safe environment of an RTS game would be a logical first step preparatory to implementing it in the real world.

Potential research questions include: What characteristics of a schema are most useful for facilitating communication in a hybrid team? How can a schema be employed to identify communication problems in a hybrid team? How can multi-level schemata support increasing levels of communication sophistication?

## 5.2 Human-machine Interaction

Trust and transparency are key elements of human-machine interaction. Within hybrid teams, heuristics such as fast and slow systems thinking (or Systems 1 and 2, as defined by Kahneman [105]) and contingent trust might have the potential to facilitate bi-directional trust and transparency to support human-machine interaction. For example, fast (System 1) thinking offers op portunities for building small cues or primes into a system that can be expected to direct human attention to one or another trust-facilitating aspects of the machine. In contrast, it might also be possible to design for a series of interactions that will influence slow (or System 2) thinking over time with a stronger, more resilient form of trust resulting. Such heuristics might be integrated within the interface between the human and autonomous agent teammates. Relevant questions that might be able to be operationalised are discussed in this section as they relate to human, machine, and the human-machine interface.

Trust and transparency must exist within a practical framework of information sharing and transactive memory. Further, human-machine interaction will be sub-optimal if the relative strengths of each discrete team member are not considered and used to best advantage. Integrating human and AI members into a team has the potential to fuse AI’s ability to find subtle patterns in large datasets that humans might miss, with the innate human ability to set those patterns into narrative contexts made all the richer for the differing perspectives brought by different members of the hybrid team [152]. By combining humans and machines in hybrid teams, such teams can achieve an appropriate balance of interoperability, authority balance, mutual learning, and trust [174].

5.2.1 Human. Humans need to know how to understand and trust their AI partners. Asking, for example, can I trust my AI teammates to act and interact in the ways I expect? Can I go into a contested space and rely on my AI teammates to provide the information to me that I need (and not a lot of information I don’t need) to make superior decisions in difficult conditions (high risk, time-critical) [51, 125]? This is particularly critical, given that when things go wrong in real world situations it will be the human who will be called upon to explain what happened. Indeed, an important role for humans in a hybrid team is risk management. Saenz et al. [174] note that humans “act as sentinels, relying on their experience to manage risky situations” and that the human partner might need to coach the AI system as a partner in a long-term relationship.

Potential research questions: Which of the components of trust for systems (e.g., competency, reliability, integrity, auditability, predictability, directability, intelligibility, effective interface, self-awareness) are necessary to achieve an “appropriate expectation” of trust within the system? Conversely, which of the above qualities are likely to create an unjustified level of trust within the system?

5.2.2 Machine. Researchers in AI and machine learning generally have been focused on improving accuracy of predictions. While prediction accuracy is important, Nguyen et al. [152] argue that models for machine learning must be built to incorporate the human element. Specifically, models such as those studied in online fact-checking must have three properties for them to be useful in practice. First, they must be transparent for humans to interpret and evaluate results. Second, they must provide support for integrating human knowledge. Third, model uncertainty must be quantified and communicated.

As part of its situational awareness, an AI team member needs to be able to monitor changes to the situation. Asking, for example, is my human teammate operating as expected and within predefined parameters? Is the human authentic or has the human been interfered with (cybersecurity)? Is the human performing at their best/usual or are they compromised (distracted, tired)? At the same time, it must assess itself to maintain the trust of its human partner. Asking, for example, am I performing at my best/usual or am I compromised (system health, battery level) [51, 125]?

Potential research questions: What parameters are required for the machine to effectively interact with its human teammate? What is the most effective way for a machine agent to predict and communicate the behaviour of others to its human teammate?

5.2.3 Interface. Following from the key aspects for AI to integrate successfully with humans noted above, interfaces need to be designed to maximise the amount of transparency of AI operations to the human team member. In Nguyen et al. [152], predictions of the AI agent in respect of potentially false online information were provided to the user, accompanied by uncertainty information, to allow the human to assess the degree to which it should be relied on. Dubey et al. [63] created a reusable interface for an AI information assistant to a human to support their proof-of-concept that was effective, though with some limitation provisos relative to the data used. As time goes by, it is likely that reusable interfaces, perhaps even standardised interfaces, can be employed in some contexts.

Interestingly, it appears that there might be a connection between one of the elements of superior decision-making, fluid intelligence (our innate ability to think and reason without prior learning), and playing video games. For example, playing **multi-player online battle arena (MOBA)** video games, such as DoTA II is correlated with fluid intelligence, especially during adolescence and early adulthood [119]. Further, playing action video games can contribute to improved visuo motor control, such as hand-to-eye coordination. For example, one study found that players of action game have better driving skills than players of non-action games [126]. Therefore, it might be possible that human performance can be improved through interaction with AI team members.

Potential research questions: Are there methods that could be employed within a humanmachine interface to build trust more swiftly? How can hybrid teammates build a shared knowledge of who is responsible for given tasks/sets of tasks? How can uncertainty in the operating environment be resolved collaboratively?

## 5.3 Distributed Decision-making

The use of modern AI in decision-making, be it in a supporting or collaborative role, is a very young discipline. Key terms and concepts are still being defined [62] and little is yet known about the mechanisms for using AI in decision-making in a spatially distributed hybrid team. This is further exacerbated when considering that these teams might need to operate in time-critical situations. Decision-making in a hybrid team is further complicated by the differences in the ways the members of the team reach decisions. For humans, the components of individual decision-making contributing to superiority include numeracy, fluid intelligence, cognitive reflection (using reasoning rather than intuition), and memory [184]. Conversely, AI reaches predictions based on correctly constructed methods (e.g., rules-based inferences or probabilistic algorithms) enabling them to operate within acceptable minima of bias and risk [69].

As there are no widely accepted definitions for distributed decision superiority in hybrid teams, we propose that it be defined as follows:

Distributed decision superiority in a human-AI hybrid team means the ability for the hybrid team to formulate a series of decisions, either collectively or individually, that lead to more successful outcomes than a comparative team.

Although the modelling described above is constrained to circumstances in which humans are the decision-makers and actuators, and AI plays a supporting role, it could be employed in situations where AI is also a decision-maker and actuator by allowing the AI to take action in areas of trust where the AI is likely to have solved correctly and the risks of acting on incorrect solutions are acceptable. A high-performing hybrid team would be characterised by effective protocols to accommodate and evaluate the performance of team members. Distributed decision-making in our research framework includes shared understanding, trust and transparency, and decision-making.

5.3.1 Shared Understanding. Shared understanding differs from shared (bi-directional) situational awareness discussed previously in that shared understanding surpasses knowledge of a situation and encompasses the knowledge of each member of the hybrid team to understand their roles and limits and knowledge of tasks. Hybrid teams need to have the ability to apply both strict and ‘fuzzy’ rules to determine a course of action [48].

Potential research questions: What are the most effective communication strategies for impacting decision efficacy within hybrid teams? How can we measure the level of shared understanding? What is the minimum shared understanding needed to enable decision-making as a team? How can a machine ensure its purpose aligns with its human teammate’s expectation? How can a human ensure their expectations align with the machine teammate’s purpose?

5.3.2 Trust and Transparency. As discussed in Section 3 above, making decisions in a hybrid team to achieve optimal outcomes is a complex process that rests upon a strong foundation of human trust and known bi-directional pathways for collaboration within a mutually understood context [60]. This mutually understood context, or group shared understanding, takes place in human teams through transactive memory [127], or the team’s collective understanding of who knows what at any given moment. As the term implies, team knowledge is a series of transactions in which appropriate information is shared at the appropriate time. As Griffin and Neale [76] note in their investigation of transactive memory, “individual information is only as valuable to the team as the process that allows it to be accessible to the team.”

Establishing communication protocols for negotiating decisions between a human and agent is a non-trivial task, with few examples in the literature on the process by which hybrid team decision-making can be effected. However, there is some prior work in this area. Traum et al. [195] modelled negotiation states in a human-simulation team using a series of stances contained in the set {committed, endorsed, mentioned, not mentioned, disparaged, rejected}. The simulation team member adopted stances as an outcome of speech or negotiation acts on the part of the human. These included accept acts on the part of the human team member that led to a committed stance on the part of the simulation team member. Similarly, reject acts produced a rejected stance.

Counter-proposal acts led to two stances: (a) disparagement of the original proposal or (b) endorsed stance towards the new proposal. Explanation acts produced either a disparaged or endorsed stance [195].

Potential research questions: How can swift trust be achieved between humans and machine teammates within a hybrid team? What heuristics could be employed within a human-machine interface to build swift trust? What is the relationship between transparency and system complexity within a hybrid team? How does the status of the trust relationship impact the risk tolerance threshold for humans in a hybrid team? Which of the components for trust are most likely to create an undeserved or risky level of trust in the system?

5.3.3 Decision-making. As with any team, a state of advanced performance in a hybrid team is not arrived at via a ‘plug and play’ modality. There are several stages that must first be navigated, each with its own challenges. A classic model that can be usefully adapted to explore these stages is Tuckman’s model of team formation [197], which divides the process of establishing a high-performing team into four stages: forming, storming, norming, and performing. The implementation of this model is well-known in co-located human teams and has relevance to teaming aspects that reflect human-AI hybridity in teaming: short-term technical teams [31] and virtual teams [104, 157].

**Forming:** The first stage of Tuckman’s model establishes relationships and organisational rules, which appears to hold true for human-AI relationships. Humans interacting with AI do not simply accept the outputs of an AI algorithm, they need knowledge about the overall purpose of the AI and details of its construction. For example, in deploying a medical AI decision model, the clinicians who were introduced to the system required “upfront information about basic, global properties of the model, such as its known strengths and limitations, its subjective point-of-view, and its overall design objective–what it’s designed to be optimized for” [31].

**Storming:** In the second stage of Tuckman’s model the complexity of the operational domains becomes clearer, as do the challenges. The human might not understand what the AI is doing and why. Amershi et al. [7] investigated potential guidelines for human-AI interaction and found that the systems that they tested in the study most frequently failed the basic guideline that the system made clear “why [it] did what it did.” Humans are also likely to interact differently with AI than with other humans. In a study to determine how humans interacted socially with AI, it was discovered that humans behaved more reservedly (repressing their personalities) when interacting with Microsoft chatbot Little Ice, which might contribute to stress and/or cognitive load [147].

**Norming:** In the norming stage of team formation, team members refine their understandings and interactions and establish ways of doing things, such as protocols, balances between competing agendas, and feedback mechanisms. The interactions between AI and human become more facile, and the hybrid team is more focused on the project at hand. During this stage, humans begin to view their AI partner as an ally [162]. A danger in this stage is over-trusting. Transparency is therefore critical to enabling human team members to understand the limits of the AI model [152] and any changes in individual AI performance that might “reduce team performance by making mistakes in regions where humans have learned to trust the AI” [17]. Being able to shift to a new perspective might then become important (e.g., Reference [186]).

**Performing:** Tuckman’s model calls for a team to reach a level of high performance in this stage. However, this stage has not yet been reported in the human-machine team literature to the best of our ability to discover. Theoretically, a hybrid team would now be an effective problem-solving team. The human would have a valid mental model of the AI’s reliability and would understand how to access transparent data about its operations to validate any areas of uncertainty.

Potential research questions: Can knowledge of the Tuckman’s model of team formation guide or assist in human-AI teams proceeding quickly to the stage of high performance? What are the differences and similarities between a decision arrived at by a human, a decision arrived at by a machine, and a decision negotiated between a human and a machine in a hybrid team? How does the adoption of negotiation stances (e.g., committed, endorsed, mentioned, not mentioned, disparaged, rejected) as a communication protocol within hybrid teams impact decision superiority? What criteria are most useful for accepting/rejecting a counter-proposal during the negotiation for decision superiority within a hybrid team? What are the most effective strategies for fusing the unique decision-making characteristics of humans and machines to achieve decision superiority in hybrid teams?

## 5.4 Human-machine Operations

As the leading edge of hybrid collaboration and teaming, the literature is almost silent on the topic of AI enacting its own decisions and actioning them, with the exception of AI control applications in autonomous land, sea, and air vehicles. However, there is significant research in the use of AI to control game play in video games. Given the superior ability of AI agents to execute a large number of actions rapidly, and the ‘superhuman’ reaction times and precision of AI agents in comparison to humans, it is unsurprising that AI team members can be superior to human team members in these aspects. In some games, AI agents have an omniscient view of the game map and no need to control a camera to view it. However, research is now questioning underlying strategies in AI, with the goal of making them more able to be interpreted by humans, thus increasing our understanding and potentially realising these novel strategies in human strategic arenas [131]. This is a fertile field for new knowledge about models and strategies for accomplishing tasks within the video game environment, which might then have applications in real-world scenarios.

The areas that will need to be investigated relate to capability, enacting decisions, and evaluating and correcting choices. Given the present state of the literature, there are many more questions than answers, though it is to be expected that research outputs on this subject will be forthcoming in future.

5.4.1 Capability. For a human-AI team to act as an operational force, that is to say that they can take decisions and act on them, the hybrid team must understand its capability and the resources and assets available to be acted upon. Potential research questions: How can a hybrid team understand what the allowable/potential control relationships are? How can a hybrid team identify available assets? How can a hybrid team incorporate and utilise additional assets?

5.4.2 Enacting Decisions. While there are many examples of AI decision enactment (automatic braking, driverless cars, high-speed trading), hybrid team decision enactment, where a human-AI team enact a decision together, or even determine which member of the hybrid team is authorised to enact a decision, is still largely an unexplored research area in relation to human-AI teams. How ever, there is a wealth of research in human-system automation. For example, in 2000, Dearden [54] posited scenarios as a basis for analysing allocation of functions between systems and human decision-makers to maximise human-machine system operation. Investigations such as these might be fruitfully explored in the context of human-AI teaming. Potential research questions: What are the most effective strategies for a hybrid team balancing decision-making resources across multiple scenario components? How can a hybrid team evaluate results at interim deci sion points to determine the usefulness of a decision? What are the most effective strategies for a hybrid team to identify how to improve the speed, efficiency, and reliability of the decision-making process?

5.4.3 Evaluating. Identifying real-time evaluation of hybrid team decisions will need to be considered as part of a decision feedback loop that allows a hybrid team to enact successive decisions and determine the efficacy of the outcomes of these decisions. Potential research questions: What are the most effective protocols for evaluating the performance of team members within a hybrid team?

5.4.4 Correcting. Where previous decisions result in sub-optimal outcomes, the hybrid team will need to be able to correct the course of action. Potential research questions: How can a hybrid team identify situation changes at decision points and changes to hybrid team capability? What are the most effective strategies for a hybrid team to enact changes to improve the speed, efficiency, and reliability of decisions?

## 5.5 Transferability

As we have seen, some of the elements that will make transferability of hybrid teams possible are knowledge transfer and exchange, the affordances of the experimental environment chosen, and the metrics and measures arising from the experimental environment that can then be mapped and evaluated to inform real-world operations of hybrid teams.

Once the human-AI teams transition to a real-world context, the core questions relate to aspects of the real-world that might have been unknown or resisted simulation. However, even where known real-world aspects have been modelled successfully in the experimental environment, it can be expected that the efficacy of the experimentally modelled outcomes will be impacted by unknown confounding factors including shifts in human perception when the human-machine operations become “real.” Given the dearth of research available on hybrid team operations, it is unsurprising that there is even less on its transferability to real-world contexts. This is therefore a significant open field for research.

Potential research questions might include: How well does the simulation map to the real-world context? To what extent do the human and AI roles shift? Will the human adapt to the real-world and possibly tailor questions to the AI? Can the human and AI collaboratively model the new context? How can new forms of knowledge be incorporated? In the new real-world context, what are the strengths and weaknesses of both human and AI? How can the metrics collected be evaluated and mapped to real-world contexts? What is the relationship between quantitative psychometric measures and physiological biometric measures when measuring trust? What is the most effective strategy for transferring knowledge between the research team and stakeholders?

## 5.6 Modelling an Agile Research Implementation Process

The next logical step after constructing a research framework is implementation. However, as Zhou points out, implementation of explainable human-AI is highly dependent on contextual fac tors [214]. Taking a flexible, iterative approach to implementing a human-AI team solution to a real-world problem means identifying the goals and component elements of the research problem. Importantly, the research goals and the criteria by which the identified research goals are subsequently evaluated are determined at the commencement of each release iteration. Once the work of the release cycle is completed, the research goals are evaluated, with the newly acquired knowledge and other outcomes informing the choice of research goals and evaluation criteria of the succeeding release. In Figure 3, we posit potential research goals as they might appear after three release cycles of a project addressing an adversarial scenario. This scenario could be combating cybercrime or a time-critical policing activity or any situation in which a bad actor poses a threat to be neutralised.

As shown in Figure 3, prior to each release cycle, the specific research goals for that iteration are identified. For example, in the first release, one element might be 3.R1, achieving the research goal of establishing decision protocols for a hybrid team to scaffold distributed decision-making. At the completion of the release cycle, the outcomes of the research are evaluated against the initial research goals defined for the iteration. In the case of 3.R1, the outcome might well have achieved the desired outcome, that is to say, that effective human-AI decision-making protocols are established, but perhaps it is noted that the protocols have limitations that might lead to over or under-reliance on AI in the decision-making process. Therefore, it is decided that the research goal of the next release with respect to hybrid team distributed decision-making, 3.R2, which might have been to identify how to highlight the most important information, will instead focus on identifying the limitations of the AI team member with the goal of establishing utilisation boundaries.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 3. Modelling a potential Agile research implementation process after the first three releases in respect of a research problem using an adversarial situation as exemplar (simplified). H = human, AI = AI agent, and hybrid means human-AI team. (A) = Pre-release research goal identification, (B) = Post-release evaluation of outcomes. R1–3 indicate three release cycles of the solution. Only one sub-area (bolded) per research area of the framework is included as an example but it is expected that tasks from all sub-areas would be incorporated in this implementation model.

It is not necessarily the case that each element of the overall project is addressed in every release. Furthermore, evaluating the outcomes of a release might result in taking a decision to eliminate or defer a research goal based on the outcomes of the preceding release. In the case of our example, the research goal of highlighting the most important information is deferred to 3.R3.

An important element of the synthesis of this release cycle is the inclusion of a transferability stage, where learning outcomes from the experimental environment are formalised and deployed to incrementally expand the working solution. This reflects the overall goal, that of testing and transferring achieved research goals to a real-world scenario to create an effective and robust AI teaming solution for that scenario.

Using a flexible, incremental Agile approach, research uncertainty is managed and research outcomes of the most value are produced. The desired outcome (in this case an effective human-AI hybrid team skilled in responding to an adversarial attack) is delivered starting with the “bare bones” of the solution, which can be evaluated for efficacy and research direction, then built upon in subsequent releases of the solution.

## 6 CONCLUSIONS

Effective human-AI teaming offers significant opportunities for improvements in team performance and decision-making, but also presents substantial challenges. One of the key challenges lies in understanding, defining, and mapping the problem space itself, which encompasses a broad range of intersecting and interacting domains. In this article, we explored and mapped the emerging field of human-AI teaming by employing an Agile approach to iteratively construct a new research framework, grounded in previous literature from a range of related topics. Our aim was to develop a new framework that researchers can use to understand and approach the many unanswered research questions that relate to this new complex and emerging field. Our resulting framework covers the areas of bi-directional situational awareness, human-AI interaction, intelligent decision-making, human-AI operations, and transferability from safe development environments to real-world contexts. Importantly, our framework provides a structure within which the process of future research in hybrid teaming can be organised and combined. Once each of the research areas is mastered, a minimum viable hybrid team can be developed. This minimum viable hybrid team can then be further developed to the point of utility in the experimental environment, and ultimately, the real world.

We found that the path of human-AI teaming, from inception to high-performing team, even in an experimental environment, covers a broad range of aspects from shared situational awareness to complex decision-making and decision-enacting processes. This research landscape is characterised less by knowledge than by open research questions. It is likely that many of the questions researchers will encounter along the way have yet to be asked, let alone answered. We have taken an important first step to plot the landmarks of this research landscape, to identify a contextual setting within which the answers to the research questions can be placed as they arise, until the topography becomes clearer and the methods for navigating it more obvious.

Our article contributes the first holistic framework that researchers can use to understand and investigate the complex and varied research questions related to human-AI teaming. Our proposed framework provides a superstructure within which future research in human-AI teaming can be situated and to which successive waves of hybrid teaming research can accrue. Further, we have highlighted the essential role of trust and transparency in successful, interpretable hybrid teaming. We also present a novel application of the Agile methodology for knowledge discovery and construction, in addition to research management.

A limitation of our investigations in developing our research framework relates to Human-Machine Operations. It might be that there are sources of insight into human-AI operations or, at least, formal speculation on this element of the framework, but it was difficult to ascertain. For now, research in real-world human-AI teams is largely in the realm of thought experiments and tangential insights. This will change in future years as hybrid teaming becomes more possible in the real world.

Our future work will employ, test, and refine our proposed framework via experimentation in a video game environment. Our ongoing work aims to demonstrate elements of bi-directional situational awareness, human-machine interaction, intelligent decision-making, and hybrid team operations for enacting superior decision-making. Through this research, we expect to identify a range of factors that can be mapped to, and evaluated for, utility in real-world contexts. Further, we will undertake deeper investigations into potential research on the topic of human-AI operations in a teaming environment, with the goal to identify, map, and evaluate elements of hybrid teaming relevant to real-world contexts.

In venturing into this broad field of unanswered research questions, we suggest that researchers bring with them a high tolerance for uncertainty and a strong and Agile methodology.
